name: ThetaHealing

lead: ThetaHealing is a meditation-based practice created by Vianna Stibal in 1995. Practitioners and clients enter a guided meditative state, identify beliefs they hold, and replace them with new ones. Proponents say shifting beliefs about self-worth, attractiveness, health or money changes how a person feels and carries themselves, which they see as part of improving how they look and present.

It is taught through certified instructors and a company, the ThetaHealing Institute of Knowledge. Research is small: one EEG study of ten healer-client pairs did not find the increase in theta-band brain activity that the method's name implies. Wikipedia classes it as a New Age practice, and critics have questioned its claims.

paras: Sessions are usually one-on-one, in person or by phone or video. The practitioner and client meditate together, the practitioner asks questions and often uses muscle testing to identify a belief, and then the belief is replaced by a new one in the meditative state. Courses at several levels certify practitioners and instructors. Followers describe effects in their own sessions as emotional rather than visible.

The main documented concern is that people with serious illness might rely on the method instead of medical care; the founder says it should be used alongside evidence-based medicine. Critics have objected to course claims about cancer and DNA, and a US court case awarded damages to former students over contract and fraud claims. Sessions carry no known physical risk. Course fees can be substantial.

Claimed change in confidence and presentation
angle.text: Proponents use ThetaHealing to work on beliefs about self-image, health and worth, and describe the result as greater confidence and a calmer, more self-assured presentation. It does not act on physical features directly.

lead: ThetaHealing is a trademarked meditation and energy-healing method created by Vianna Stibal, an American naturopath, in 1995. It is based on the idea that conscious and unconscious beliefs shape emotional well-being and, in turn, physical health. [1]

People who use it for self-improvement say that changing limiting beliefs, for example about self-worth or attractiveness, changes confidence, posture and the way a person presents themselves, which is the route by which it connects to appearance. This is the practitioners' account; it is not a treatment for any physical feature.[2]

Teaching and certification run through the ThetaHealing Institute of Knowledge (THInK), which states that instructors teach in more than 150 countries.[1] One published EEG study did not detect the increase in theta-frequency activity that practitioners describe, and critics including researchers at McGill University and Edzard Ernst have criticised the method.[3][1]

paras: The method is built around a meditative state in which practitioners say they reach the theta brainwave range, then use prayer and visualisation to connect with what Stibal calls the Creator of All That Is. In that state, a belief that is thought to hold the client back is identified and replaced.[2][1]

Sessions are usually one-on-one, with the practitioner listening and asking questions. They can be held remotely. Practitioners often use applied kinesiology (muscle testing) to find beliefs.[1] Stibal also describes a framework of seven planes of existence.[1]

Stibal reports that she developed the technique in 1995 while facing a serious illness, which she says resolved after she entered the theta state. Independent medical confirmation of this account is not available, and Grokipedia notes it rests on the founder's own materials.[2]

She began certifying instructors around 2000, published a book in 2006, and in 2008 founded the ThetaHealing Institute of Knowledge in Montana, with online courses added in 2020.[2] The organisation reports activity in well over 100 countries.[2][1]

Practitioners hold that beliefs operate at several levels, including core, genetic, historical and soul levels, and that changing them in the theta state can change emotional and physical patterns.[2] Some courses also teach topics such as DNA activation and the idea that money is an illusion, which critics have singled out.[1]
In the founder's account, the technique is intended to be used alongside evidence-based medicine.[1]

A 2016 study in the Journal of Alternative and Complementary Medicine recorded EEGs from ten healers and ten clients across ten sessions. Theta activity did not increase, and the theta-2 band decreased in healers during sessions; small correlations and phase synchronies between healer and client were seen. The authors concluded the hypothesis that the method generates more theta activity could not be confirmed, and noted that this says nothing about other effects of the method.[3] No published trial has tested ThetaHealing for appearance, confidence or health outcomes.

Edzard Ernst has described the method as unsupported by evidence, and the McGill University Office for Science and Society reported that theta activity overall went down during sessions.[1] Critics also object to claims about cancer made by some course providers.[1]

In a lawsuit filed in 2014, two former students sued Stibal and THInK; a jury awarded damages on contract and fraud claims, and the punitive award was reduced on appeal, with an Idaho Supreme Court decision in 2016.[1]

timeline.event: Stibal publishes her book on the method.[2]
ThetaHealing Institute of Knowledge founded in Montana.[2]
Former students file suit against Stibal and THInK.[1]
EEG study published; Idaho Supreme Court rules in the lawsuit.[3][1]
